title: Examine social features as pertaining to the workplace

lessons.title: Selecting and examining a sociological feature
lessons.html:
Sociology at work

A sociological feature is a pattern in society that shapes how people live and work. In South African workplaces, including farms, packhouses, co-operatives and extension offices, important features include:

  • Gender: roles of women and men, women's access to land, credit and leadership.
  • Race and the legacy of apartheid: land ownership patterns, skills gaps, the history of farm labour relations.
  • Language and culture: many home languages on one farm, different customs and beliefs.
  • Age and youth unemployment: young people leaving rural areas, ageing farmers.
  • HIV and AIDS and other health issues: absenteeism, stigma, loss of skilled workers.
  • Migration: seasonal workers, workers from neighbouring countries, people moving to towns.
  • Poverty and inequality: low wages, food insecurity, housing on farms.
  • Disability: access to work and facilities.

Choosing a feature and justifying it

Select a feature that clearly affects your workplace and that you can find information about. Justify it with evidence: workplace statistics (staff numbers by gender in each job level), observation, interviews, Stats SA data for your district, and organisational reports. For example: On our citrus farm 70 percent of seasonal pickers are women, but only one of eight supervisors is a woman. This makes gender a relevant feature to examine.

Examining the workplace

Look at the feature across the workplace:

AreaQuestions to ask
RecruitmentWho gets hired for which jobs, and why?
Pay and conditionsAre there differences between groups for similar work?
Training and promotionWho gets sent on courses and promoted?
CommunicationIn which language are meetings and notices?
FacilitiesAre toilets, housing and transport suitable for everyone?
CultureWhat jokes, attitudes and informal rules exist?

Be careful to describe what you find fairly, using evidence rather than assumptions or stereotypes.

lessons.title: Constitutional, legal and policy context
lessons.html:
The framework for fair workplaces

The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, is the supreme law. Its Bill of Rights includes equality, human dignity, freedom of association, fair labour practices and the right to an environment not harmful to health. All workplace laws and policies must be consistent with it.

Key legislation

LawRelevance
Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995Fair dismissal, unions, dispute resolution through the CCMA
Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997Working hours, leave, minimum conditions; sectoral determinations and the national minimum wage apply to farm workers
Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998Prohibits unfair discrimination; designated employers must take affirmative action measures
Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act 4 of 2000Unfair discrimination outside the employment relationship as well
Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993Safe working conditions
Skills Development Act 97 of 1998Training, SETAs such as AgriSETA, learnerships

Land reform, tenure security legislation for farm dwellers, and B-BBEE codes (including the AgriBEE sector code) also shape agricultural workplaces.

Analysing the issues

For your chosen feature, ask:

  • What rights does the Constitution give the people affected?
  • Which laws and policies apply, and what do they require of the employer?
  • Is the workplace complying, or is there a gap between law and practice?
  • Are there tensions, for example between seasonal production needs and fair working hours, or between cultural practices and gender equality?

Example: Under the Employment Equity Act, unfair discrimination on the grounds of gender, pregnancy or family responsibility is prohibited. If women pickers are never considered for supervisor posts, the farm should examine its promotion practices and could set equity targets and offer supervisor training.

Remember that the law sets the minimum. Good workplace practice often goes further, for example by providing childcare during harvest or HIV awareness programmes.

lessons.title: Impact on individuals and groups, and personal reflection
lessons.html:
How social features affect people at work

Social features affect individuals and groups in different ways.

  • Individuals may experience exclusion, low self-esteem, stress, harassment or limited career growth, or, where the workplace is fair, motivation, loyalty and confidence.
  • Groups may form along lines of language, origin or gender. This can bring support and solidarity, but also cliques, conflict and distrust between groups, such as between local and migrant workers.
  • The organisation is affected through productivity, staff turnover, labour disputes, reputation with buyers (many export markets audit social compliance) and its ability to attract skilled staff.

Case example

A vegetable farm employs local workers and seasonal workers from a neighbouring province. Instructions are given only in Afrikaans, which many seasonal workers do not understand well. Mistakes in harvesting increase, local workers complain that seasonal workers are lazy, and tension grows. When the farm appoints interpreters, uses pictures on work instructions and holds a joint team meeting, mistakes drop and relations improve. The feature, language and migration, affected individuals (frustration, blame), groups (us and them) and the business (losses).

Reflecting on implications for yourself

Examining social features is not only about others. Ask yourself:

  1. What are my own assumptions about people of a different gender, age, culture or origin?
  2. How have social features affected my own opportunities?
  3. How do my words and actions as a supervisor or extension officer include or exclude people?
  4. What can I change in my own practice: languages I use, who I invite to meetings, who I recommend for training?

Write down two or three specific actions, for example inviting women farmers to speak first at a study group, or learning greetings in the home languages of your team.

Key points

  • Social features such as gender, language, migration, health and inequality shape South African workplaces.
  • Select a feature using workplace evidence, not stereotypes.
  • The Constitution and labour laws set minimum standards for fair workplaces.
  • Social features affect individuals, groups and the organisation's performance.
  • Reflect on your own assumptions and commit to specific actions.
